newsitem.title: USA: Derivative users reject new accounting rule - survey.
newsitem.headline: Derivative users reject new accounting rule - survey.

text.p: Most firms using derivatives oppose a proposal by the Financial Accounting Standards Board to revise derivatives accounting, according to the results of a survey done by KPMG Peat Marwick.

Only 18 percent of the 139 financial and non-financial firms responding said the FASB proposal would be an improvement over current practice, while 86 percent said they preferred existing rules, KPMG reported.
The survey, sponsored by two major derivatives dealers, J.P. Morgan & Co and Citicorp, was sent to 700 firms asking about the FASB's exposure draft released in June.
The survey followed a dispute between members of the FASB and bank officials over accounting practices for derivatives.
"At one meeting, there was a disagreement about the diversity of practice for accounting for derivatives," Frank Taylor, senior manager in KPMG's department of professional practice, said.

So the banks decided to distribute a survey to members of the Fortune 500, as well as members of organizations such as Securities Industry Association and Treasury Management Association, Taylor said.
The survey found great uniformity of practice in accounting for derivatives transactions, Taylor added.
More than 90 percent of companies responding said they match the accounting of derivatives with the economics of the transaction involving the financial instrument.

And 96 percent said they require correlation between the effects of the derivative and any item hedged by the derivative. About 91 percent require the derivative to be linked to a specific asset or homogenous pool.
And 99 percent require that derivative instruments be designated and documented as relating to a particular risk management strategy in order to qualify for risk management accounting.
The FASB proposal would limit the use of hedge accounting for many common hedging transactions currently allowed, such as sale of floating-rate debt combined with a floating-to-fixed rate swap.
FASB officials did not return a call for comment Friday afternoon.
